sections.b: The Book of the Watchers is the oldest full account of angels who sinned. Two hundred "children of heaven," led by Semyaza, swear an oath on Mount Hermon, take human wives and father giants (1 Enoch 6–7). Asael or Azazel teaches weapons and cosmetics, and others teach magic and star-lore (1 Enoch 8). At the archangels' plea, God has Raphael bind Azazel in the desert and Michael bind Semyaza's band under the earth for seventy generations, until the fire of judgment (1 Enoch 10:4–13). The Watchers ask Enoch to plead for them; God refuses, because spirits who never die had no need of wives and should have prayed for humans, not the reverse (1 Enoch 13–15).

sections.h: From 1 Enoch to the New Testament
sections.b: Jude 6 (angels who "deserted the dwelling that was theirs," kept in chains in darkness) and 2 Peter 2:4 (angels thrown into Tartarus, kept for judgment) match 1 Enoch 10 and 12:4 closely. 1 Peter 3:19–20, on "spirits in prison" who disobeyed in Noah's day, is read by many scholars against 1 Enoch 13–16, where Enoch announces judgment to the imprisoned Watchers. Others read 1 Peter as Christ preaching through Noah, or to the human dead.

common: Most scholars date the Watchers' story in 1 Enoch 6–16 to the 200s BC or earlier, and think Jude and 2 Peter knew it.
Most think 1 Enoch 6–11 combines a Semyaza story and an Azazel story.
uncommon: J. T. Milik argued that Genesis 6:1–4 abbreviates an older Enoch story, not the reverse.
Some read the Watchers as a coded attack on Jerusalem priests who married outside the rules (David Suter).

sections.b: 1 Enoch calls the children of angels and women "huge giants," 3,000 cubits tall, who eat everything people produce and then the people themselves (1 Enoch 7:2–5). Syncellus's Greek lists three generations: giants, Nephilim and Elioud. God has Gabriel set them against each other (1 Enoch 10:9–10). When they die, their spirits become evil spirits on the earth (1 Enoch 15:8–16:1). A separate Aramaic Book of Giants from Qumran tells their side of the story.

common: Many scholars read the devouring giants as a picture of the warring Greek kings who followed Alexander the Great.

sections.h: The Book of the Watchers (1 Enoch 1–36)
sections.b: The first part of 1 Enoch tells how Enoch was hidden with the angels (1 Enoch 12:1–2), sent as "the scribe of righteousness" to announce judgment to the fallen Watchers (1 Enoch 12–16), taken up to God's throne (1 Enoch 14), and guided by archangels to the ends of the earth, the prisons of the angels, the places of the dead, the throne mountain and the garden of Eden (1 Enoch 17–36). Its opening oracle of judgment (1 Enoch 1:9) is the verse Jude 14–15 quotes. Aramaic copies from Qumran (4Q201–202) show that it existed by the early 100s BC.

common: Most scholars date chapters 6–36 to the 200s BC and chapters 1–5 to about 200 BC.

sections.h: Evil spirits from the giants (1 Enoch 15–16)
sections.b: 1 Enoch gives the oldest Jewish account of where demons come from. The giants were born of spirit and flesh; when they died, their spirits came out of their bodies and became "evil spirits on the earth." They trouble, attack and destroy, eat nothing, cannot be seen, and rise against humans, until the great judgment (1 Enoch 15:8–16:1). Jubilees 10 and Qumran prayers against "the spirits of the bastards" take up the idea. Justin Martyr and Athenagoras repeated it; later Christian teaching mostly held that demons are the fallen angels themselves.

1 Enoch 22 divides the dead into separate places inside a western mountain until the judgment: the righteous by a bright spring, sinners not judged in life, the murdered who plead like Abel, and sinners who will not be raised. It is the oldest Jewish text we have that sorts the dead before the final judgment, a step between the shadowy Sheol of the Psalms and the divided Hades of Luke 16.

sections.h: The earliest ascent to the throne (1 Enoch 14)
sections.b: Enoch is carried by clouds and winds past a wall of hailstones into a house of hail and fire, and then into a greater house where "the Great Glory" sits on a throne like frost, with wheels like the sun, cherubim, and rivers of fire flowing out beneath (1 Enoch 14:8–23). The scene is probably older than Daniel 7:9–10, which shares many of its details, and it stands at the head of Jewish throne-mysticism and of Revelation 4.

sections.h: The tree on God's mountain (1 Enoch 24–25)
sections.b: On the middle of seven mountains, God's throne, Enoch sees a tree whose scent surpasses all others and whose leaves never wither. Michael tells him that no one may touch it until the great judgment; then it will be given to the righteous, planted by the house of the Lord, and its fruit will give life to the chosen (1 Enoch 24:4–25:6). The Book of the Watchers also places a separate tree of wisdom in the garden in the east (1 Enoch 32:3–6).

sections.h: Azazel bound in the desert (1 Enoch 10)
sections.b: In 1 Enoch the fallen angel Azazel is bound hand and foot, thrown into darkness in the desert of Dudael under sharp rocks, and "every sin" is written against him (1 Enoch 10:4–8). Many scholars think this draws on the Day of Atonement, when a goat chosen "for Azazel" carried Israel's sins into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:8–10, 21–22) and, according to the Mishnah, was pushed off a cliff (Mishnah Yoma 6:6) after reaching the wilderness at Beit Ḥiddudo (Yoma 6:8). The Greek of 1 Enoch spells the desert Dadouēl.

sections.h: The prisons at the end of the world (1 Enoch 18–21)
sections.b: Enoch sees two prisons. At the end of heaven and earth, where there is no sky above and no ground below, seven stars burn as punishment for not rising at their times, bound for ten thousand years (1 Enoch 18:12–16; 21:1–6). Beyond it is a chasm of falling fire, "the prison of the angels," where they are held forever (1 Enoch 21:7–10). The Greek calls the realm Uriel rules "Tartarus" (1 Enoch 20:2), the word 2 Peter 2:4 uses.

sections.h: The cursed valley by Jerusalem (1 Enoch 27)
sections.b: The Book of the Watchers makes the valley beside Jerusalem the place where those who speak against God will be gathered and judged forever, in sight of the righteous (1 Enoch 27:1–4). It is the Valley of Hinnom, where children had been burned (Jeremiah 7:31–32), and the earliest text that makes it the place of final judgment: the Gehenna of Jesus' warnings.

sections.h: Archangels in the Book of the Watchers
sections.b: 1 Enoch 9:1 names four archangels, Michael, Uriel, Raphael and Gabriel (the Ge'ez has different names), who plead for the earth and then carry out God's orders: Uriel warns Noah, Raphael binds Azazel, Gabriel destroys the giants, and Michael binds Semyaza (1 Enoch 10). Chapter 20 lists seven holy angels with their charges, and they guide Enoch on his journeys (1 Enoch 21–36).

Far to the east, beyond the Red Sea and the angel Zotiel, Enoch reaches "the Garden of Righteousness" and sees the tree of wisdom from which Adam and Eve ate (1 Enoch 32:3–6). It is the only mention of Adam and Eve in the Book of the Watchers, which traces the world's evil chiefly to the fallen angels.

Jude 14–15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9 and calls it Enoch's prophecy. Compared word by word, Jude's wording is very close to the Greek form of the verse, including the "harsh words" that sinners spoke, which the Gizeh Greek and the Aramaic of 4Q204 also have but the Ge'ez lacks. Jude shortens the Greek and adds "the Lord"; with the Ge'ez he has "look" and a past tense. The Ethiopian Orthodox churches take the quotation as confirming 1 Enoch as Scripture; most other churches say quoting a book does not make it canonical.

sections.h: No angel could look at his face (1 Enoch 14)
sections.b: In Enoch's throne vision none of the angels can come near or look at God's face, and "no flesh" can see him; Enoch lies face down and only hears God's voice (1 Enoch 14:21–25). The scene keeps the rule of Exodus 33:20 even in heaven.
